newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany's Stark dampens hopes for broad EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany's Stark dampens hopes for broad EMU.

text.p: Germany on Tuesday played down expectations that Europe's single currency will begin with a big starting lineup in 1999, urging strict compliance to convergence goals to ensure the euro is stable.

Juergen Stark, State Secretary at the Finance Ministry, said some aspirants should forsake the political prestige of joining economic and monetary union (EMU) at the outset. They should instead watch from the sidelines until they are ready to join.
"There are members whose economic structures are not yet well enough prepared to take part," Stark told a conference of German newspaper editors outside Bonn.

Even some countries which qualify on paper "would be well advised to maintain exchange rate flexibility for a certain period, and...respect that they should not have to follow the rigid rules of the European Central Bank from the start."
Stark, number two to Finance Minister Theo Waigel and a hard-liner on monetary union, is seen as Chancellor Helmut Kohl's man at the ministry because he comes from the same Christian Democrat party.
He did not name names, but his comments appeared directed at countries like Italy or Spain that have not yet established a track record of exchange rate stability.

"For me the markets have overdone expectations that a large number of countries can qualify," Stark said. "We have to make sure that these countries also stand for stability. Only then does this project have a lasting chance of success."
Stark said Germany would meet the criteria this year to qualify for EMU despite revising up its budget deficit forecast due to higher unemployment.

A government annual economic forecast officially published on Tuesday forecast the budget deficit this year at 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). Waigel's 1997 budget, passed late last year, assumed a 2.5 percent deficit.
Stark said that Germany would not overshoot the three percent limit set by the Maastricht Treaty for joining EMU, which is due to be launched in 1999.
"I believe and I am convinced that we will meet the Maastricht criteria in 1997. We are open and honest," he said.
He added that the calm within the European exchange rate mechanism was an indication that financial markets were betting on a broad-based EMU.

"There are certain expectations in the market that a large number of European countries are going to start. There is calm in the exchange rate mechanism. It's being speculated that this is already a foregone conclusion," he said.
"I believe that there can be no foregone conclusions. The point of no return is in 1998."
The eligibility of European Union states to join will be judged early next year, and Stark said as many as 14 of the 15 EU members could meet the Maastricht budget deficit target.
Stark gave no direct comment on whether he expected EMU to go ahead on schedule, but said: "Fundamentally, stability still comes before the timetable."
He also moved foreign exchange markets with a comment that recent dollar gains were merely a correction to excessive mark strength over the past two years.
"In the dollar I see a normalisation of the strong overvaluation of the deutschemark in 1995 and '96," he said.
The U.S. currency climbed after Stark's comment to 31-month highs against the mark. In mid-afternoon European trading it stood at 1.6530/40 marks.
